title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop changes verifier-detected safety violations of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal (requested model: gpt-5-mini) produced once per task, and (2) guarded — the identical shared LLM proposal examined by a deterministic netops validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) with up to one automated repair iteration invoked only if the validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. The preregistered exact McNemar two-sided test implemented as the exact binomial on discordant pairs yields two-sided p = 1.00; one-sided p for testing guarded>baseline = 0.5. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Interpretation: on this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; measured marginal verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is therefore small, though the single archived discordant episode shows the loop corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks that translate operator intent into device configuration, plan multi-step changes, and propose repair sequences. System descriptions and recent surveys emphasize that operational safety typically depends more on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback—than on the model alone [https://doi.org/10.1145/3098822.3098834; https://doi.org/10.1145/3718958.3750537; http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729]. A recurring mitigation pattern is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): the model generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties, and an automated or human-in-the-loop repair completes or aborts the change. Despite conceptual consensus, there is limited controlled, preregistered measurement that isolates the verifier’s marginal contribution when holding the model’s initial proposal fixed.

We therefore preregistered and executed a paired experiment that isolates verifier+repair impact under canonical, verifier-scoped synthetic workload semantics. The study asks a narrowly operational question (end of this paragraph): given identical initial proposals (shared-initial_candidate semantics), how much does integrating a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM alone? The restriction to shared-initial semantics intentionally conditions on identical model proposals to quantify the verifier’s marginal corrective effect independent of verifier-guided regeneration strategies.
sections.related_work:
Deterministic verification tooling and formal analyses for network configurations (header-space analysis and route-model verifiers) can check reachability, isolation, and update-safety and underpin much prior NetOps verification work [https://doi.org/10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Recent NetOps/AIOps systems employ or recommend LLM-based intent translators and stress the necessity of validators and guardrails to attain operational reliability [https://doi.org/10.1145/3718958.3750537; http://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05557; http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729]. Across structured-generation domains, generate–verify–repair and critic-in-the-loop patterns are widely proposed to reduce incorrect outputs and to enable machine-checkable guarantees. Failure-mode studies of LLM-driven automation document hallucination, overconfidence, and tool-integration errors, motivating verifier-in-the-loop pipelines [https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6484501; http://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05557].

However, few controlled ablations quantify a verifier’s effect size under deterministic, reproducible conditions that fix the model’s proposal. Our work contributes such a preregistered, artifact-backed measurement and situates it within this literature: it quantifies the marginal corrective power of a verifier+single-repair when the model’s initial candidate is held constant, clarifying what that mitigation buys in low-error regimes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan: The preregistration (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) froze the research question, inclusion/exclusion rules, task-generation seeds, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rule prior to execution. Confirmatory hypothesis H1: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback, using a paired within-task comparison. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations.

Task generation and strata: We used the archived deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with preregistered seeds to generate a deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks. Tasks were stratified: VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), static-route-change (166). To preserve construct validity relative to the verifier, the generator constrained allowed_fields to {admin, mtu, vlan}. Tasks referencing verifier-unmodeled features would have been routed to an 'unmodeled-feature' cohort and excluded per the preregistration; no confirmatory exclusions occurred. Each task includes initial_state, expected_final_state, and an explicit required_sequence; representative task payloads and seeds are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Generation semantics and experimental control: The preregistered generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" and independent_condition_generation = false. For each task a single shared LLM proposal (the shared candidate) was produced and recorded; the baseline condition uses that recorded proposal as the reported LLM output, while the guarded condition validates that same proposal and invokes the repair-stage provider call only if the deterministic validator reports a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. This isolates the verifier+repair marginal effect conditional on identical proposals and avoids confounding with verifier-guided regeneration.

Models, adapter, and validator: Requested model = gpt-5-mini called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses). Model configuration is archived in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini", max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation semantics). The deterministic validator used for gating and scoring is deterministic_netops_validator_v5; its specification and the validator violation-code→severity mapping are archived in the execution artifacts. The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per preregistered contract.

Primary test: exact McNemar on paired binary outcomes. Implementation detail (exact convention used): let n10 be the count of pairs where guarded = 1 (pass) and baseline = 0 (fail), and n01 the count where guarded = 0 and baseline = 1. Let n = n10 + n01 (discordant pairs). The archived executor implements the two-sided exact McNemar by performing an exact binomial test on n10 with X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5) and computing the two-sided p as p_two_sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)}, truncated at 1.0. This is equivalent to the common exact McNemar two-sided binomial tail rule for small n and is recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. For reporting completeness we also compute the one-sided tail probability P(X ≥ n10) when testing the directional alternative guarded>baseline.

Bootstrap CI: We computed paired-bootstrap percentile CIs for the absolute success-rate difference using B = 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729, resampling unit = task/pair while preserving pairing. The resampling draws 500 pairs with replacement per bootstrap replicate; the bootstrap distribution of guarded_rate − baseline_rate yields the percentile CI reported.

Missingness, retry policy, and stopping rule: The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automated retries for transient model-provider errors. The run stopped when the preregistered confirmatory pairs (N = 500) completed or when the adapter model-call budget was reached. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 501, completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 pairs × 2 conditions recorded under shared-initial semantics with one repair-stage call), and failed_episode_count = 0. All provider calls, retries, and timestamps are archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary outcomes: The experiment completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair-stage calls = 1). Aggregated per-condition counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency (guarded × baseline) is n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Exact McNemar two-sided result and interpretation: With n = n10 + n01 = 1 discordant pair and n10 = 1, the archived exact-binomial two-sided rule yields p_two_sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ 1), P(X ≥ 1)} where X ∼ Binomial(1, 0.5). Evaluating these tails gives min{1.0, 0.5} = 0.5 and thus p_two_sided = 1.0 (conventional truncation applied). The one-sided tail for testing guarded>baseline equals P(X ≥ 1) = 0.5. These exact probabilities are straightforward consequences of the small discordant sample size. We therefore report two-sided p = 1.00 (archived executor convention) and one-sided p = 0.5; the paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference (B = 10,000, seed = 1729, paired resampling) is [0.0, 0.006]. All numeric artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) are archived.

Repair activity and discordant-pair provenance: Observed repair-stage provider calls = 1 across the entire execution. That single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1): the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The execution and scoring artifacts archive per-task validator diagnostics, normalized configurations, and the repair prompt/response for the invoked repair. The raw results file execution/raw_results.jsonl is the deterministic source for locating the discordant episode: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair entries where baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while guarded scoring indicates pass == 1. Because exactly one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, that deterministic filter returns the single episode and its repair-stage provider-call trace; the validator violation codes and repair prompt/response for that episode are preserved in the archived per-task record.

Secondary and subgroup analyses: The preregistered per-violation-class secondary analyses were uninformative because observed violation counts were nearly zero—no meaningful class-level counts supported inference. The preregistration assumed a substantially higher baseline prevalence (planning baseline p_b ≈ 0.30 for power calculations); the realized baseline error prevalence (1/500 failures) created a ceiling effect that reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains on the pass-rate metric. The archived power plan, sensitivity analyses, and multiplicity controls are available in the preregistration and analysis artifacts; they document that the planned power assumptions did not hold given the observed error rate.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation: This experiment quantifies the marginal verifier+single-repair effect under a constrained, well-specified operational regime: a single requested model (gpt-5-mini), shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic validator modeling a limited feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and a single automated repair iteration. In that regime the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals, so the measured absolute effect on the pass-rate metric is small (0.002). Importantly, this outcome should not be read as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary: (1) the verifier produced a concrete correction (the single discordant episode), demonstrating corrective potential; (2) in workloads with higher baseline error prevalence, broader property coverage, or heterogeneous vendor CLIs, verifier+repair gains could be larger.

Design-choice implications: The shared_initial_candidate semantic was preregistered to isolate verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals; it answers the specific operational question: how much additional safety does a verifier+single-repair provide when the model’s proposed change is fixed? It does not measure different deployment semantics—e.g., verifier-guided regeneration, multiple repair iterations, or cost-weighted optimization between generations and repairs—each of which addresses different operational tradeoffs and could yield larger final-pass probabilities. Practitioners must align experimental semantics with deployment semantics when estimating guardrail benefits.

Statistical considerations and ceiling effects: Small discordant-pair counts (n ≤ 1) produce trivial exact two-sided p-values under the archived two-sided binomial convention; for n = 1 the two-sided exact McNemar p = 1.0 regardless of the direction of the single discordant. The paired-bootstrap CI (B = 10,000) provides a complementary uncertainty quantification for the absolute difference and illustrates that zero remains a plausible value given the data (95% CI lower bound = 0.0). The preregistered power calculation assumed baseline p_b ≈ 0.30; observed baseline ≈ 0.998 invalidated that assumption and produced low power to detect small absolute improvements. Future studies should calibrate task difficulty to the verifier’s modeled property coverage to avoid extreme ceiling effects for the primary estimand.

Operational recommendations grounded in the archive: (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative operational data before committing large repair budgets—when baseline error is already very low, marginal pass-rate gains from expensive verifier+repair pipelines may be small. (2) Prefer verifier designs whose modeled property set aligns with the operator’s safety-critical constraints; the archived validator-spec and mapping files document what was modeled here. (3) Choose generation semantics (shared-initial vs verifier-guided regeneration) to match deployment priorities: shared-initial semantics minimize model re-generation cost while verifier-guided strategies may maximize final-pass probability at the expense of extra model calls.

Reproducibility and how to inspect the archived corrected episode: The evidence bundle contains the complete preregistration, task generators and seeds, model-configuration, provider-call traces, raw LLM responses, validator traces, repair prompts/responses, execution logs, analysis CSVs, and the deterministic reconciliation manifest (execution/* and analysis/* artifacts). To inspect the single discordant episode deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for entries where baseline scoring indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) and guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; because exactly one such discordant pair exists, that filter returns the single archive record and its repair-stage trace. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived alongside the validator-spec artifacts in the bundle and documents which violation codes were treated as high/medium severity for scoring.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the supplied synthetic verifier-scoped corpus and with the requested model/validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the two-sided binomial convention implemented). The result documents a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal error prevalence is extremely low and verifier coverage is constrained, the measurable marginal pass-rate benefit of a verifier on this metric may be negligible, though the verifier can still correct rare but concrete failures (one archived corrected episode). Operators should measure baseline error prevalence and verifier coverage on representative workloads and align generation/repair semantics with operational priorities. The archived evidence bundle supports deterministic re-inspection of every primary claim made here.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; the task payloads in the archive show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 must be interpreted in that context and reflects the archived two-sided exact-binomial convention for n = 1 discordant pair.
